passages.text: DIAMOND, the most valuable and the hardest of all precious stones, which cuts and scratches all others, and is itself cut only by its own dust.
Diamonds are found only in the East Indies, chiefly in the kingdoms of Golconda and Visapour, and in Brazil, where they were first discovered in the present century.
They are found in the earth, or in the sand of rivers; and it is said that a mine, when worked out, yields new diamonds after some years, as if they grew again.
Sir Isaac Newton, observing its great power of refracting light, conjectured that the diamond is an unctuous substance coagulated, and therefore probably combustible.
This was confirmed by the Florentine academicians, who in 1694 exposed diamonds to the focus of a great burning-glass, and saw them consumed so that nothing remained.
Mr Lavoisier afterwards found that a diamond, burned in a close vessel, yields fixed air, as charcoal does.
Yet its nature is still unknown; most writers rank it among the crystals, as a stone formed of an earth peculiar to itself.
Diamond is a solid form of the element carbon with its atoms arranged in a crystal structure called diamond cubic. It has the highest hardness of any natural material.
Diamonds were first mined in India, which was the main source for centuries. Brazil became a major source after diamonds were found there in the 1720s.
Today the largest producers of diamonds include Russia, Botswana, Canada and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Large deposits were found in South Africa from 1867.
Most natural diamonds form at high temperature and pressure in the Earth's mantle, about 150 to 250 kilometres deep. Most are between 1 billion and 3.5 billion years old.
Volcanic rocks called kimberlites carry diamonds to the surface. Erosion frees the diamonds, and rivers carry them into gravel and sand, where many have been found.

Isaac Newton noted that diamond bends light very strongly, as oily substances do, and suggested that it could burn. In 1694 scientists in Florence made a diamond vanish with the heat of a large burning lens.
In 1772 Antoine Lavoisier showed that burning diamond produces carbon dioxide. In 1797 Smithson Tennant showed that diamond is made of carbon alone.

reasons: Rare terms appear in both: hardest, India, Brazil, burning-glass, Newton.
Carbon scores well but covers the element, not the stone.

alignments.label: Hardest of stones

britannica.quote: the hardest of all precious stones

wikipedia.quote: It has the highest hardness of any natural material

alignments.note: The claim holds. Wikipedia extends it from precious stones to all natural materials.

alignments.label: Only India and Brazil

britannica.quote: Diamonds are found only in the East Indies

wikipedia.quote: Today the largest producers of diamonds include Russia, Botswana, Canada and the Democratic Republic of the Congo

alignments.note: True for what Europeans knew in 1797. The large finds in Africa, Russia and Canada came later.

alignments.label: Found in river sand

wikipedia.quote: rivers carry them into gravel and sand, where many have been found

alignments.note: The observation holds. Wikipedia adds how the diamonds got there: erosion of the rock that carried them up.

alignments.label: Diamonds grow again

britannica.quote: a mine, when worked out, yields new diamonds after some years, as if they grew again

wikipedia.quote: Most are between 1 billion and 3.5 billion years old

alignments.note: A change in knowledge. Diamonds do not grow back in a mine. Inference: new stones in an old mine came from more digging or from rain washing out loose ground.

alignments.label: Newton's guess

britannica.quote: conjectured that the diamond is an unctuous substance coagulated, and therefore probably combustible

alignments.note: A change in language. An unctuous substance is an oily one. Newton's guess proved right.

alignments.label: Burned by a burning-glass

britannica.quote: in 1694 exposed diamonds to the focus of a great burning-glass, and saw them consumed

wikipedia.quote: In 1694 scientists in Florence made a diamond vanish with the heat of a large burning lens

alignments.note: The same experiment, with the same date and place.

alignments.label: Yields fixed air

britannica.quote: yields fixed air, as charcoal does

alignments.note: A change in language. Fixed air is the old name for carbon dioxide.

alignments.label: A peculiar earth

britannica.quote: a stone formed of an earth peculiar to itself

wikipedia.quote: diamond is made of carbon alone

alignments.note: A change in knowledge. Tennant published his result in 1797, too late for this entry. Diamond is pure carbon, the same element as charcoal.

alignments.label: Formed in the mantle

wikipedia.quote: form at high temperature and pressure in the Earth's mantle, about 150 to 250 kilometres deep

alignments.note: New knowledge. The 1797 entry says nothing about how or where diamonds form.

suggestedQuestions: What did the 1797 entry know about what diamond is made of?
Where did the 1797 entry say diamonds are found?
Who first showed that diamond burns?

What did the 1797 entry know about what.answer: It knew that diamond burns [B5] and that it gives fixed air when burned, as charcoal does [B6]. But it still called its nature unknown and ranked it among crystals [B7]. Wikipedia says diamond is a form of carbon [W1]. Tennant showed this in 1797 [W7].

Where did the 1797 entry say diamonds ar.answer: Only in the East Indies and Brazil [B2], in the earth or in river sand [B3]. Wikipedia agrees that India and then Brazil were the early sources [W2], but today the largest producers include Russia, Botswana, Canada and the Democratic Republic of the Congo [W3].

Who first showed that diamond burns?.answer: Newton guessed it could burn [B4] [W6]. Scientists in Florence burned diamonds with a large burning-glass in 1694 [B5] [W6]. Lavoisier then showed that the burning gives fixed air, which is carbon dioxide [B6] [W7].
